stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Mrs. Bennet eagerly shares news of a wealthy, unmarried newcomer whom she hopes will marry one of her daughters, while Mr. Bennet responds with apparent indifference.
Mr. Bennet is eager to meet Mr. Bingley because he hopes to buy Netherfield Park from him.
Mrs. Bennet and Mrs. Long argue about which family should be allowed to rent Netherfield Park.
Mr. Bingley explains to the Bennets why he has decided to move to their neighborhood.

rationale.A: Choice A is the best answer because the text centers on Mrs. Bennet's excited report that "a young man of large fortune" has rented Netherfield and her hope that he will marry "one of them," while Mr. Bennet "made no answer" and asks questions that frustrate her.
rationale.B: Choice B is incorrect because Mr. Bennet shows no eagerness to meet Mr. Bingley, and the text says Bingley has rented Netherfield; it doesn't mention Mr. Bennet wanting to buy it.
rationale.C: Choice C is incorrect because Mrs. Long only brings Mrs. Bennet the news; the text doesn't present any argument between them.
rationale.D: Choice D is incorrect because Mr. Bingley never appears or speaks in the text; his plans are reported secondhand by Mrs. Bennet.

stem: As used in the text, what does the word “fixed” most nearly mean?
choices: Repaired
Firmly established
Arranged in advance
Motionless

rationale.A: Choice A is incorrect because the text says the "truth" about wealthy single men is "so well fixed in the minds of the surrounding families" that they treat such a man as a future son-in-law. In this context, "fixed" means firmly established: the belief is settled in their minds.
rationale.B: Choice B is the best answer because nothing in the text has been broken or needs repair; the word describes how firmly a belief is held.
rationale.C: Choice C is incorrect because although "fixed" can mean rigged or prearranged, the text describes a belief that families hold, not an outcome someone arranged.
rationale.D: Choice D is incorrect because the text is describing a belief in people's minds, not physical stillness.

excerpt: However little known the feelings or views of such a man may be on his first entering a neighbourhood, this truth is so well fixed in the minds of the surrounding families, that he is considered the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters.

stem: Which choice best describes the function of the first sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It presents a general claim, with evident irony, that the conversation between Mr. and Mrs. Bennet then illustrates.
It introduces the narrator as a character who plans to marry Mr. Bingley.
It provides historical background about property laws in England.
It summarizes the disagreement between Mr. and Mrs. Bennet that the text later resolves.

rationale.A: Choice A is the best answer because the opening sentence states, as a "truth universally acknowledged," that a rich single man "must be in want of a wife." The following dialogue shows that it is really the neighborhood families, like Mrs. Bennet, who want him to have a wife, so the claim is ironic, and the conversation illustrates it.
rationale.B: Choice B is incorrect because the narrator isn't a character in the text and expresses no plan to marry anyone.
rationale.C: Choice C is incorrect because the sentence makes a claim about social attitudes toward marriage, not about laws.
rationale.D: Choice D is incorrect because the first sentence doesn't summarize the Bennets' conversation, and the text doesn't resolve their disagreement.

stem: Which quotation from the text most effectively illustrates the claim that Mr. Bennet teases his wife by pretending not to understand her intentions?
choices: "Mr. Bennet replied that he had not."
"How so? How can it affect them?"
"What is his name?"
"This was invitation enough."

rationale.A: Choice A is incorrect because Mrs. Bennet has just said that a rich single man is "a fine thing for our girls," and Mr. Bennet asks how it could "affect them," as though her meaning weren't obvious. Her reply, "how can you be so tiresome!", shows that he is pretending not to understand.
rationale.B: Choice B is the best answer because this is a direct answer to a factual question about whether he had heard the news; it doesn't show him pretending not to understand.
rationale.C: Choice C is incorrect because this is a simple request for information, not a pretense of confusion about Mrs. Bennet's intentions.
rationale.D: Choice D is incorrect because this is the narrator's comment on Mrs. Bennet's readiness to share her news, not something Mr. Bennet says.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: families that
families. That
families; that
families, that,

rationale.A: Choice A is the best answer because the clause beginning with "that" completes the construction "so well fixed ... that," and no punctuation is needed between "families" and "that." (Austen's 1813 text has a comma here, following older punctuation habits; current Standard English conventions don't use one.)
rationale.B: Choice B is incorrect because a period creates a fragment beginning with "That he is considered..." and breaks the "so ... that" construction.
rationale.C: Choice C is incorrect because a semicolon is used to join two independent clauses, but "that he is considered..." is a dependent clause.
rationale.D: Choice D is incorrect because punctuation isn't used between the subordinating conjunction "that" and the subject of its clause, "he."

excerpt: However little known the feelings or views of such a man may be on his first entering a neighbourhood, this truth is so well fixed in the minds of the surrounding ______ he is considered the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters.

stem: As used in the text, what does the word “proposition” most nearly mean?
choices: Offer
Principle
Plan
Request

rationale.A: Choice A is incorrect because Lincoln says the nation was "dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal." In this context, a proposition is a principle or idea that the nation is committed to.
rationale.B: Choice B is the best answer because "proposition" can mean a business offer, but the nation isn't dedicated to an offer.
rationale.C: Choice C is incorrect because the equality of all people is presented as a principle, not as a plan of action.
rationale.D: Choice D is incorrect because the text presents equality as a founding idea, not as something being asked for.

excerpt: Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation, conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To urge listeners to honor the soldiers who died by continuing the work for which they fought
To describe the military strategy used during the battle
To explain why the battlefield should not be used as a cemetery
To celebrate the end of the civil war

rationale.A: Choice A is the best answer because after acknowledging that the soldiers have already "consecrated" the field, Lincoln says "it is for us the living ... to be dedicated here to the unfinished work" and resolves "that these dead shall not have died in vain." The text's purpose is to call listeners to continue that work.
rationale.B: Choice B is incorrect because the text doesn't discuss any military strategy.
rationale.C: Choice C is incorrect because the text says it is "fitting and proper" to dedicate part of the field "as a final resting place," so it supports the cemetery.
rationale.D: Choice D is incorrect because Lincoln says "we are engaged in a great civil war," so the war hasn't ended.

stem: According to the text, why does Lincoln say that he and the audience cannot consecrate the ground?
choices: The soldiers who fought there have already consecrated it through their actions.
The government has not yet purchased the land.
Too few people attended the ceremony.
The nation has not yet won the war.

rationale.A: Choice A is the best answer because Lincoln explains that "the brave men, living and dead, who struggled here, have consecrated it, far above our poor power to add or detract."
rationale.B: Choice B is incorrect because the text doesn't mention who owns the land.
rationale.C: Choice C is incorrect because the text doesn't comment on the size of the audience.
rationale.D: Choice D is incorrect because although the war is ongoing, Lincoln's stated reason is that the soldiers have already consecrated the ground.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: But,
Therefore,
Similarly,
For example,

rationale.A: Choice A is the best answer because the previous sentence says it is "fitting and proper" to dedicate the field, and the next sentence says that, "in a larger sense," the speakers "can not dedicate" the ground. "But" signals this contrast.
rationale.B: Choice B is incorrect because "Therefore" signals a result, but being unable to dedicate the ground isn't a result of its being fitting to do so.
rationale.C: Choice C is incorrect because "Similarly" signals a comparable idea, but the sentence qualifies, rather than repeats, the previous claim.
rationale.D: Choice D is incorrect because "For example" introduces an illustration, but the sentence doesn't give an example of the previous claim.

excerpt: It is altogether fitting and proper that we should do this. ______ in a larger sense, we can not dedicate—we can not consecrate—we can not hallow—this ground.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: have
has
having
to have

rationale.A: Choice A is the best answer because the plural subject of the sentence, "The brave men," requires the plural verb "have."
rationale.B: Choice B is incorrect because "has" is singular and doesn't agree with the plural subject "men."
rationale.C: Choice C is incorrect because "having" doesn't provide the sentence with a main verb, resulting in a fragment.
rationale.D: Choice D is incorrect because "to have" doesn't provide the sentence with a main verb, resulting in a fragment.

excerpt: The brave men, living and dead, who struggled here, ______ consecrated it, far above our poor power to add or detract.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The variety of life visible in an ordinary scene has been produced by natural laws, a view the author finds grand.
Living things compete so fiercely that most forms of life will soon become extinct.
The laws that govern living things are the same as the law of gravity.
Insects and worms are more important to an ecosystem than plants or birds.

rationale.A: Choice A is the best answer because the author describes a bank full of plants, birds, insects, and worms, says these forms "have all been produced by laws acting around us," and concludes, "There is grandeur in this view of life."
rationale.B: Choice B is incorrect because the text mentions the "Extinction of less-improved forms" as one consequence of natural selection, but it doesn't claim most life will soon become extinct.
rationale.C: Choice C is incorrect because the author compares the planet's motion under "the fixed law of gravity" with the evolution of life, but he doesn't say the laws are the same.
rationale.D: Choice D is incorrect because the text presents these organisms as "dependent on each other"; it doesn't rank their importance.

stem: As used in the text, what does the word “exalted” most nearly mean?
choices: Noble
Excited
Exaggerated
Recent

rationale.A: Choice A is the best answer because Darwin calls the production of the higher animals "the most exalted object which we are capable of conceiving," meaning the most noble or elevated thing we can imagine.
rationale.B: Choice B is incorrect because "exalted" can describe a joyful state of mind, but here it describes an object of thought, not a feeling.
rationale.C: Choice C is incorrect because the text doesn't suggest that anything is overstated.
rationale.D: Choice D is incorrect because "exalted" refers to value or rank, not to time.

excerpt: Thus, from the war of nature, from famine and death, the most exalted object which we are capable of conceiving, namely, the production of the higher animals, directly follows.

stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It describes a familiar natural scene, identifies the laws that produced it, and ends by reflecting on the significance of this view.
It presents a hypothesis, describes an experiment to test it, and reports the results.
It summarizes a debate between rival scientists and declares one of them correct.
It lists objections to a theory and responds to each in turn.

rationale.A: Choice A is the best answer because the text opens with the "entangled bank," then names the laws ("Growth with Reproduction," "Inheritance," and so on) that produced its life forms, and closes by stating, "There is grandeur in this view of life."
rationale.B: Choice B is incorrect because the text doesn't describe an experiment.
rationale.C: Choice C is incorrect because no other scientists are mentioned in the text.
rationale.D: Choice D is incorrect because the text doesn't raise or respond to objections.

stem: Based on the text, what can most reasonably be inferred about the organisms on the “entangled bank”?
choices: Their survival is linked through complex interactions with one another.
They developed independently, with no influence on one another.
They all belong to a single species.
They will remain unchanged over time.

rationale.A: Choice A is the best answer because Darwin describes the organisms as "dependent on each other in so complex a manner," which suggests that their survival is linked through their interactions.
rationale.B: Choice B is incorrect because the text says the organisms are "dependent on each other," which contradicts the idea that they developed with no influence on one another.
rationale.C: Choice C is incorrect because the text describes "many plants of many kinds," as well as birds, insects, and worms, so the organisms belong to many species.
rationale.D: Choice D is incorrect because the text says forms "have been, and are being, evolved," which indicates continuing change.

excerpt: It is interesting to contemplate an entangled bank, clothed with many plants of many kinds, with birds singing on the bushes, with various insects flitting about, and with worms crawling through the damp earth, and to reflect that these elaborately constructed forms, so different from each other, and dependent on each other in so complex a manner, have all been produced by laws acting around us.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: conceiving,
conceiving;
conceiving.
conceiving

rationale.A: Choice A is the best answer because the phrase "namely, the production of the higher animals" renames "object" and is a supplementary element. It must be set off by a pair of commas, and the comma after "conceiving" is the first of that pair.
rationale.B: Choice B is incorrect because a semicolon would separate the subject "object" from its verb "follows."
rationale.C: Choice C is incorrect because a period would separate the subject "object" from its verb "follows," creating two fragments.
rationale.D: Choice D is incorrect because without a comma, the supplementary phrase isn't set off from the rest of the sentence; only the comma after "animals" would remain.

excerpt: Thus, from the war of nature, from famine and death, the most exalted object which we are capable of ______ namely, the production of the higher animals, directly follows.

stem: As used in the text, what does the word “deliberately” most nearly mean?
choices: Slowly
Intentionally and thoughtfully
Stubbornly
Secretly

rationale.A: Choice A is incorrect because the narrator explains that he wanted "to front only the essential facts of life" and learn "what it had to teach." Living "deliberately" means living with intention and careful thought.
rationale.B: Choice B is the best answer because "deliberately" can describe an unhurried pace, but the narrator is describing a purposeful way of living, not a speed.
rationale.C: Choice C is incorrect because the text doesn't suggest the narrator wanted to resist others or refuse to change.
rationale.D: Choice D is incorrect because the narrator plans to "publish" what he learns, which contradicts the idea of secrecy.

excerpt: I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The narrator went to live in the woods to find out, through direct experience, what is essential in life.
The narrator went to the woods to escape his debts.
The narrator went to the woods to study the plants that grow there.
The narrator argues that everyone should leave their towns and live in the woods.

rationale.A: Choice A is the best answer because the narrator says he went to the woods to "front only the essential facts of life" and to know life "by experience."
rationale.B: Choice B is incorrect because the text doesn't mention debts.
rationale.C: Choice C is incorrect because the text doesn't mention studying plants; the narrator's focus is on life itself.
rationale.D: Choice D is incorrect because the narrator explains his own reasons; he doesn't argue that others should do the same.

stem: Which quotation from the text most effectively illustrates the claim that the narrator wanted to judge life based on his own experience rather than on others' conclusions?
choices: "if it were sublime, to know it by experience, and be able to give a true account of it in my next excursion"
"I did not wish to live what was not life, living is so dear"
"to cut a broad swath and shave close"
"nor did I wish to practise resignation, unless it was quite necessary"

rationale.A: Choice A is the best answer because the narrator wants "to know it by experience" and then give "a true account of it," which directly expresses a wish to judge life from his own experience.
rationale.B: Choice B is incorrect because this expresses how much the narrator values life, but it doesn't address how he will judge it.
rationale.C: Choice C is incorrect because this image describes living fully and closely, but it doesn't contrast his own experience with others' conclusions.
rationale.D: Choice D is incorrect because this expresses an unwillingness to give up, not a desire to judge life by experience.

stem: The narrator mentions that most men “have somewhat hastily concluded” what the chief end of man is mainly to
choices: contrast his own careful, experience-based inquiry with others' quick acceptance of a received answer.
show that he agrees with the common view of life's purpose.
prove that religious explanations of life are false.
explain why he eventually left the woods.

rationale.A: Choice A is the best answer because the word "hastily" contrasts with the narrator's goal of living "deliberately" and knowing life "by experience"; most men, he says, are "in a strange uncertainty" yet accept a ready-made answer.
rationale.B: Choice B is incorrect because by calling their conclusion hasty, the narrator distances himself from the common view rather than agreeing with it.
rationale.C: Choice C is incorrect because the narrator describes uncertainty "whether it is of the devil or of God"; he doesn't try to prove religious explanations false.
rationale.D: Choice D is incorrect because the text doesn't discuss the narrator leaving the woods.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: was
were
are being
have been

rationale.A: Choice A is the best answer because the singular pronoun "all," used here to mean everything, takes the singular verb "was," and the past tense is consistent with "wanted" earlier in the sentence.
rationale.B: Choice B is incorrect because "were" is a plural verb and doesn't agree with the singular "all."
rationale.C: Choice C is incorrect because "are being" is present progressive, which is inconsistent with the past-tense narration.
rationale.D: Choice D is incorrect because "have been" is plural and present perfect, which is inconsistent with the singular subject and the past-tense narration.

excerpt: I wanted to live deep and suck out all the marrow of life, to live so sturdily and Spartan-like as to put to rout all that ______ not life, to cut a broad swath and shave close...
